catalog_quote: There is, in Kunibidji, a well established phoneme of vowel length combined with major stress. There are numerous minimal pairs supporting the existence of such a phoneme, and further evidence is provided by the movement of this phoneme within verbal and nominal words, in some cases triggering the operation of phonological rules geminating or leniting root initial stops ... this phoneme can occur in or move to each of the following positions depending on the verb involved: root initial, root final (and other positions in the root), pronominal prefix initial, -yaka- prefix initial, -ko- prefix, suffix initial and penultimate of suffix. ... It can be seen that none of these vowel length/stress positions is word final. Word initial, prefix initial, root initial and suffix initial are possible. Root final is possible but only when not at the same time word final. No suffix final long vowels…

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Ndjébbana is a phoneme: 'major stress' fused with vowel length, marked with an acute accent in the orthography, and contrastive (numerous minimal pairs, e.g. kabála 'he ate it' vs kabbála 'boat', p. 133). Its position is not predictable from the word shape: it is a lexical/morphological property of the verb or morpheme and may sit on the root-initial, root-final, prefix-initial or suffix syllable. The only general constraint is that it never falls on the word-final syllable; where the underlying (root-final) length would be word-final it is realised on the word-initial syllable instead, and reappears root-finally when a suffix follows ('stress shifting'). Unstressed vowels tend to reduce to a/schwa. McKay explicitly contrasts this with Burarra, where stress is predictable root-initial (p. 134).
new_statements.secondary_stress: McKay 1984 'Stop alternations', p. 109: the phonemic stress 'is not the only type of stress to be found in Ndjebbana words, but it is the only phonemically significant stress and the only one coupled with lengthening of the vowel'; no rule for the non-phonemic stresses is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifting is regular but McKay calls the analysis speculative and 'a great deal more study' needed (p. 134); the verb yiyi 'leave' has one form where length does not move to the root-final under suffixation (pp. 133-134); a number of verbs have invariant stress inconsistent with the gemination rules (Stop alternations, sec. 2.2, p. 110). Clause-final syllable lengthening is a separate intonational phenomenon (grammar notes, p. 149).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, established from verb paradigms and nominal forms (whole prefixed words, i.e. the phonological word including bound pronominal prefixes and suffixes); minimal pairs are cited at word level. Sentence-final lengthening is treated separately as intonation.
new_statements.identity_note: McKay's 'Ndjébbana (Kunibidji)' = Glottolog Djeebbana djee1236 (ISO djj); older names Gunavidji/Gunibidji/Djeebbana. McKay 1984 mentions inland vs coastal dialects only for a morphosyntactic choice; the stress statement is for the language as spoken at Maningrida, no dialect restriction stated.

sources.note: Section 3 'Shifting of word final vowel length' (pp. 131-134): Ndjébbana has a well-established phoneme of vowel length combined with major stress, with numerous minimal pairs; its position varies by verb and morpheme (root-initial, root-final, prefix-initial, suffix-initial, suffix-penultimate) but is never word-final; underlying word-final length shifts to word-initial position; contrasts with Burarra where stress is predictable root-initial.
